performance-fatigability.short: The measurable drop in what a muscle or person can do (maximal force, power, time to task failure) for a given task. One of the two sides of fatigue in Enoka and Duchateau's framework.

perceived-fatigability.short: How tired a person feels during a task: sensations of effort and fatigue, measured only by self-report. The other side of fatigue, next to performance fatigability.

task-failure.short: The moment a person can no longer keep up the task as set (a pace, a power, a hold). Fatigue usually starts long before it.

central-governor.short: Noakes' idea that the brain regulates exercise, partly without awareness, so that it ends before harm to the body. Debated.

peripheral-fatigue.short: Loss of force or power that comes from changes at or beyond the neuromuscular junction: the fibre's electrical signal, Ca²⁺ release or the cross-bridges.

reactive-oxygen-species.short: Highly reactive oxygen-containing molecules made in working muscle. In small amounts they are normal signals; in large amounts they can weaken contraction.

central-fatigue.short: Loss of force because the nervous system drives the muscle less: from the motor cortex (supraspinal) or in the spinal cord. Shown as a fall in voluntary activation.

voluntary-activation.short: How fully the nervous system drives a muscle in a maximal effort, in %. 100% means an electrical shock to the nerve adds no extra force.

twitch-interpolation.short: Giving a strong electrical shock to a muscle's nerve during a maximal contraction. Any extra twitch shows force the brain didn't use; it gives voluntary activation.

group-iii-iv-afferents.short: Thin sensory nerve fibres in muscle that sense metabolites and pressure and report to the spinal cord and brain. Their feedback can lower the drive to the muscle.

hypoglycaemia.short: Low blood glucose. In cyclists riding 3 h without carbohydrate it fell to about 2.5 mmol·L⁻¹ just before they had to stop.

durability.short: How early and how much an athlete's physiological profile (thresholds, power, economy) worsens during prolonged exercise.

low-frequency-fatigue.short: A loss of force that shows mainly when the muscle is stimulated at low rates (about 10–20 Hz) and lasts hours after exercise. Probably caused by impaired excitation–contraction coupling.
